summary: Describes the functions of Session Border Controllers, SIP intermediaries used by operators, with attention to practices that conflict with SIP architecture. It also looks at the operator needs behind these functions to identify protocol requirements. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Guards at the phone network's border do many jobs, and this lists them and why companies want them, even where they bend the rules.

questions: what is a session border controller
what does an sbc do in sip
why do sbcs break end to end security
subtitle: A catalogue of what Session Border Controllers do to SIP traffic, why operators want it, and where it bends SIP's rules.

tldr.problem: SIP networks grew faster than the standards that operators needed, so vendors built Session Border Controllers (SBCs) with proprietary tricks that often break SIP's end-to-end design.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes seven common SBC functions, the operator need behind each, the architectural problems each causes, and a simplified example. It then derives three requirements for future SIP standards work.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational requirements document, not a protocol. It says users cannot tell an SBC from a man-in-the-middle attacker, and it calls for SIP-friendly ways to hide topology, steer media and fix capability mismatches.

today: RFC 5853 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. It records SBC practices and requirements as of April 2010 and defines no protocol.

sections.title: What an SBC Is and Where It Sits
sections.content:
The term Session Border Controller (SBC) is not standardized or defined anywhere. The RFC uses it for SIP intermediaries that usually sit between two service provider networks, or between an access network and a backbone network. They handle both signaling and media.

SBCs often change SIP headers and message bodies that proxies are not allowed to change, so they are by definition B2BUAs (Back-to-Back User Agents). The RFC calls the side an SBC protects the inner network and the other side the outer network.

Two scenarios recur. In peering, two operators exchange traffic and the SBC shields the receiving operator's gateways and softswitches. In access, endpoints use the SBC as their outbound proxy, and it routes requests onward to proxies in the operator network.
sections.plainLanguage: An SBC is a doorman standing between your building and the street. Everything coming in or out goes past the doorman first.

sections.title: Topology Hiding and Media Management
sections.content:
Topology hiding limits what outsiders learn about an operator's network. The common form strips Via and Record-Route headers, replaces the Contact header, and may even change Call-IDs. Operators want it to avoid exposing equipment to DoS attacks, to hide which carriers they use, or to hide their internal architecture.

Media traffic management works by rewriting the session description so that media flows through a relay the operator controls. That lets operators enforce allowed codecs, support billing models, monitor traffic, and carry out legal interception. An SBC on the media path can also notice media stopping and send BYE to both sides to clean up the "lost BYE" case.

Both functions modify messages without the user agents' consent. Neither endpoint can tell the SBC from a man-in-the-middle attacker, and the changes conflict with Authenticated Identity Management (RFC 4474) and with end-to-end encryption of message bodies.

Media relaying can also break ECN and Path MTU Discovery if the ToS, ECN and Don't Fragment fields are not handled correctly, and it can create a bottleneck at a central point. Because SBCs must understand every SDP extension, they can slow the adoption of new services.
sections.plainLanguage: The doorman can cover up the names on the mailboxes and make every phone call go through his own desk. That keeps the building safe, but you can no longer be sure who is really listening.

sections.title: Fixing Mismatches, NAT Bindings and Protocol Repair
sections.content:
Capability mismatch fixing lets user agents with different abilities talk, for example plain SIP to a 3GPP network, IPv4 to IPv6, or different codecs. The RFC calls it fragile in the long term, because the number of incompatibilities in network elements keeps growing.

Keeping NAT bindings alive is done in one described method by lowering the expiry time in a REGISTER 200 OK, so the user agent re-registers before the NAT closes its pinhole. The RFC's example changes expires=3600 to expires=60, and notes that some SBCs use a small value such as 15 seconds. Guessing a media peer's address by snooping on another stream can let an attacker divert traffic.

Protocol repair fixes messages from not-fully-compliant clients, for example rewriting lr as lr=true for older stacks. For header fields the RFC sees this as mostly compatible with SIP's end-to-end model, but repairing SDP bodies is incompatible with Authenticated Identity Management and S/MIME.
sections.plainLanguage: The doorman also translates between visitors who speak different languages, keeps the mailbox flap from closing by asking you to check in often, and quietly fixes badly written notes.

sections.title: Access Control and Media Encryption
sections.content:
Access control lets an operator decide which signaling and media its network carries. A typical setup puts firewalls in front of the inner network that accept SIP only from the SBC. On limited access links, an SBC can estimate bandwidth from the codecs in SDP and reject sessions before the link is over-subscribed. Because it handles all SIP messages, it has scalability limits and is a single point of failure, though many SBCs support redundancy.

Media encryption means the media is encrypted (for example with SRTP) only on the outer side and carried unencrypted inside, which lets an operator offer customers encryption while still doing legal interception. The RFC notes this is the same as a classical MITM attack, with the same architectural issues as media traffic management.
sections.plainLanguage: The doorman only lets in people on the list and can lock and unlock the packages as they pass through. If the doorman fails, the whole entrance stops working.

sections.title: Derived Requirements for SIP Standards
sections.content:
The RFC derives three requirements from the functions that break SIP principles when the SBC lacks the user's consent:

  • Req-1: a SIP-friendly way to hide network topology information.
  • Req-2: a SIP-friendly way to direct media traffic through intermediaries.
  • Req-3: a SIP-friendly way to fix capability mismatches in SIP messages.

Req-1 and Req-3 had no standardized solution when the RFC was written. For Req-2 it points to ongoing IETF work on SIP session policies, TURN and ICE, and says future work is still needed.

The security section adds that SBCs prevent end-to-end authentication, since user agents must tolerate actions that look like MITM attacks, and that a crashed or attacked SBC leaves ongoing sessions with undetermined behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors say: there should be better, politer ways to do these jobs, so people do not need a doorman who reads and rewrites everyone's mail.

items.title: Topology hiding
items.text: Strip and replace headers that reveal the operator's network.

items.title: Media traffic management
items.text: Rewrite session descriptions to steer media through a relay.

items.title: Capability mismatches
items.text: Connect user agents with different IP versions, codecs or extensions.

items.title: NAT bindings
items.text: Make endpoints re-register so NAT pinholes stay open.

items.title: Access control
items.text: Admit only authorized signaling and media.

items.title: Media encryption
items.text: Encrypt on the outer side and carry plain media inside.
